beforeRecord.q: Net tax revenue is $240 and government purchases are $290. What is public saving?

beforeRecord.feedback: Public saving is T − G, so $240 − $290 = −$50 under the stated net-tax convention.

afterRecord.q: Net tax revenue is $240, government purchases are $290, and private saving is $180. What is national saving, and how does the government budget affect it?
options: $130; the budget deficit reduces national saving.
$230; the budget deficit raises national saving.
$180; public saving does not enter national saving.
−$50; national saving equals public saving alone.
afterRecord.commonError: Treating public saving as the whole of national saving or reversing the deficit sign.
afterRecord.feedback: Public saving is T − G = $240 − $290 = −$50. National saving adds private and public saving: $180 − $50 = $130. The deficit reduces the total.

changes.rationale: Distinguish an ordinary application from its one-step repair counterpart.
changes.economicsRationale: Public saving is 240−290=−50. With private saving 180, national saving is 130.

It guarantees assets never fall in value.
It prevents banks from making loans.
It makes reserves unnecessary.

Higher leverage requires a larger capital cushion.
Asset losses reduce deposits before bank capital.
Borrowing protects bank capital from asset losses.

beforeRecord.q: If the Fed wants looser money but also raises interest on reserves, what tension does this create?
options: It injects reserves but may also encourage banks to hold them instead of lending.
It lowers reserves and forces banks to lend more.
It turns deposits into commodity money.
It makes fiscal policy impossible.
beforeRecord.commonError: assuming all policy tools point in the same direction
beforeRecord.feedback: More reserves can support lending, but higher interest on reserves may make banks sit on those reserves.

afterRecord.q: The Fed adds reserves to support easier credit but raises the interest rate paid on reserve balances. Why might the higher reserve rate work against its objective?
options: It raises the return banks require from alternative lending.
It automatically removes the newly added reserve balances.
It lowers the return banks require from alternative lending.
It reduces the reserve requirement on bank deposits.
afterRecord.commonError: assuming all policy tools point in the same direction
afterRecord.feedback: A higher return on reserve balances raises the opportunity cost of alternative lending and puts upward pressure on short-term rates. Adding reserves therefore does not by itself establish that credit conditions will ease.

changes.rationale: Ask a direct policy-incentive question with parallel, economically related alternatives.
changes.economicsRationale: IOR raises the return available on reserves and puts upward pressure on market rates; adding reserves need not guarantee easing.

beforeRecord.q: The Fed buys bonds while also increasing interest on reserves. Which answer best captures the policy conflict?
options: Bond purchases add reserves, but higher interest on reserves may reduce banks' willingness to lend them.
Bond purchases remove reserves, while higher interest on reserves forces banks to lend more.
Both actions clearly reduce reserves and contract lending.
Both actions clearly eliminate money demand.
beforeRecord.commonError: assuming every Fed action in a scenario pushes the same direction
beforeRecord.feedback: Buying bonds is expansionary, but higher interest on reserves can make banks hold reserves instead of lending them.

afterRecord.q: The Fed buys bonds while raising the interest rate paid on reserve balances. Which conclusion follows?
options: Reserves rise, but the reserve-rate increase pushes short-term rates upward.
Reserves fall, and both actions push short-term rates downward.
Reserves rise, so short-term rates must fall despite the reserve-rate increase.
Reserves stay fixed because the higher reserve rate cancels the purchases.
afterRecord.commonError: assuming every Fed action in a scenario pushes the same direction
afterRecord.feedback: Bond purchases add reserve balances. Raising the rate paid on those balances puts upward pressure on short-term market rates. The reserve increase alone does not establish the net effect on lending or spending.

changes.rationale: Separate the effects of the two policy instruments without saying reserves are lent to the public.
changes.economicsRationale: Bond purchases add reserve balances. Higher IOR puts upward pressure on short-term rates, so reserve quantity alone does not identify the stance.

beforeRecord.q: Which policy package most strongly reduces bank lending capacity?
options: Fed sells bonds, raises reserve requirements, and raises interest on reserves.
Fed buys bonds, lowers reserve requirements, and lowers interest on reserves.
Fed buys bonds and lowers the discount rate.
Fed lowers reserve requirements and buys bonds.
beforeRecord.commonError: failing to combine multiple contractionary tools
beforeRecord.feedback: Selling bonds drains reserves, higher reserve requirements restrict lending, and higher interest on reserves encourages banks to hold reserves.

afterRecord.q: In a hypothetical scarce-reserves system with a binding reserve requirement, which package combines actions that reduce lending capacity with incentives to reduce lending?
options: Fed sells bonds, raises reserve requirements, and raises interest on reserves.
Fed buys bonds, lowers reserve requirements, and lowers interest on reserves.
Fed buys bonds and lowers the discount rate.
Fed lowers reserve requirements and buys bonds.
afterRecord.commonError: failing to combine multiple contractionary tools
afterRecord.feedback: Bond sales reduce reserves and a higher reserve requirement reduces lending capacity in this model. A higher return on reserve balances also makes alternative lending less attractive.

changes.rationale: State the hypothetical framework and distinguish capacity from incentives.
changes.economicsRationale: Reserve requirements constrain expansion in this stipulated model; IOR changes the relative return to lending, not the legal reserve requirement.

beforeRecord.q: Which policy package most strongly expands bank lending capacity?
options: Fed buys bonds, lowers reserve requirements, and lowers interest on reserves.
Fed sells bonds, raises reserve requirements, and raises interest on reserves.
Fed sells bonds and raises the discount rate.
Fed raises reserve requirements and pays banks more to hold reserves.
beforeRecord.commonError: missing that lower interest on reserves can encourage lending
beforeRecord.feedback: Buying bonds adds reserves, lower reserve requirements free reserves, and lower interest on reserves weakens the incentive to sit on reserves.

afterRecord.q: In a hypothetical scarce-reserves system with a binding reserve requirement, which package combines actions that expand lending capacity with incentives to expand lending?
options: Fed buys bonds, lowers reserve requirements, and lowers interest on reserves.
Fed sells bonds, raises reserve requirements, and raises interest on reserves.
Fed sells bonds and raises the discount rate.
Fed raises reserve requirements and pays banks more to hold reserves.
afterRecord.commonError: missing that lower interest on reserves can encourage lending
afterRecord.feedback: Bond purchases add reserves and a lower reserve requirement increases lending capacity in this model. A lower return on reserve balances also makes alternative lending more attractive.

changes.rationale: State the hypothetical framework and distinguish capacity from incentives.
changes.economicsRationale: Reserve requirements constrain expansion in this stipulated model; IOR changes the relative return to lending, not the legal reserve requirement.

options: Higher money demand pushes the rate down and higher supply pushes it down; the effects reinforce
Higher money demand pushes the rate up and higher supply pushes it down; opposite directions ensure an unchanged rate
Higher money demand pushes the rate up and higher supply pushes it down; relative shifts determine the result
Higher money demand pushes the rate up and higher supply pushes it up; the effects reinforce
beforeRecord.commonError: Assuming one shift always dominates.
beforeRecord.feedback: When money demand and money supply both increase, the interest-rate effect depends on which shift is larger.

afterRecord.q: In the textbook liquidity-preference model, money demand rises while money supply increases. What can be concluded about the equilibrium interest rate?

Higher money demand pushes the rate up and higher supply pushes it down; opposite directions ensure an unchanged rate
Higher money demand pushes the rate up and higher supply pushes it down; relative shifts determine the result
Higher money demand pushes the rate up and higher supply pushes it up; the effects reinforce
afterRecord.commonError: Assuming one shift always dominates.
afterRecord.feedback: When money demand and money supply both increase, the interest-rate effect depends on which shift is larger.

Neutrality applies only to fiscal policy and never to money.
Neutrality means the Phillips curve slopes downward in the long run.

beforeRecord.q: A student says, 'If the Fed buys bonds, inflation must rise immediately and real output cannot move.' Which correction is strongest?
options: In the short run, lower rates can raise AD and output before long-run price adjustment dominates.
Bond purchases only change fiscal spending, so inflation and output are unaffected.
Bond purchases lower AD because reserves rise and lending must fall.
In the long run, bond purchases permanently reduce unemployment.
beforeRecord.commonError: Skipping the short-run transmission channel.
beforeRecord.feedback: Open-market purchases lower interest rates and can raise AD and output in the short run.

In the long run, bond purchases permanently reduce unemployment.

beforeRecord.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
beforeRecord.q: If the labor force is 150 million and the adult population is 200 million, what is the labor force participation rate?
beforeRecord.feedback: Labor force participation = 150 / 200 x 100 = 75%.

afterRecord.commonError: Confusing adults outside the labor force with unemployed active job seekers.
afterRecord.q: The labor force is 150 million and the adult population is 200 million. What is the labor-force participation rate, and what does the remaining share represent?
options: 75%; the remaining 25% are all unemployed.
50%; the remaining 50% are outside the labor force.
75%; the remaining 25% are outside the labor force.
66.7%; the remaining 33.3% are all unemployed.
afterRecord.feedback: LFPR = 150/200 × 100 = 75%. The remaining 50 million adults are outside the labor force. Unemployed people who are actively seeking work belong to the labor force.

changes.rationale: Extend the repeated LFPR arithmetic to interpretation at its existing Medium tier.
changes.economicsRationale: 150/200=75%; the complement is outside the labor force, not necessarily unemployed.

beforeRecord.q: Nominal wage contracts for 20 workers are fixed. Actual output prices rise unexpectedly while other input prices are unchanged. Which initial response and later qualification are consistent with the sticky-wage account?
options: The actual price rise shifts SRAS left immediately because higher revenues reduce profitable output
Lower real labor cost supports movement up SRAS; later wage resetting can shift SRAS left
Higher real labor cost supports movement down SRAS; later wage resetting shifts SRAS right
The actual price rise immediately shifts LRAS right; nominal contracts determine long-run capacity
beforeRecord.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The actual price rise shifts SRAS left immediately because higher revenues reduce profitable output” in this short run aggregate supply task.
beforeRecord.feedback: With wages fixed, higher output prices lower real wage cost and encourage output along SRAS. Later higher nominal wages/expected prices change the schedule rather than repeating the same movement.

afterRecord.q: Firms sign new contracts that raise nominal wages. Productivity and other input prices are unchanged. What happens to short-run aggregate supply?
options: It shifts right.
It shifts left.
There is only a movement up the unchanged curve.
There is only a movement down the unchanged curve.
afterRecord.commonError: Treating a change in nominal input costs as movement along an unchanged SRAS curve.
afterRecord.feedback: Higher nominal wages raise firms’ production costs at each price level, shifting short-run aggregate supply left.

changes.rationale: Restore a direct SRAS-shifter recognition task for the first checkpoint instead of duplicating a later two-horizon question.
changes.economicsRationale: Higher contracted nominal wages raise production costs at each output price and shift SRAS left.

beforeRecord.q: Nominal wage contracts for 60 workers are fixed. Actual output prices rise unexpectedly while other input prices are unchanged. Which initial response and later qualification are consistent with the sticky-wage account?
options: The actual price rise immediately shifts LRAS right; nominal contracts determine long-run capacity
The actual price rise shifts SRAS left immediately because higher revenues reduce profitable output
Lower real labor cost supports movement up SRAS; later wage resetting can shift SRAS left
Higher real labor cost supports movement down SRAS; later wage resetting shifts SRAS right
beforeRecord.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The actual price rise immediately shifts LRAS right; nominal contracts determine long-run capacity” in this short run aggregate supply task.
beforeRecord.feedback: With wages fixed, higher output prices lower real wage cost and encourage output along SRAS. Later higher nominal wages/expected prices change the schedule rather than repeating the same movement.

The actual price rise shifts SRAS left immediately because higher revenues reduce profitable output

Higher real labor cost supports movement down SRAS; later wage resetting shifts SRAS right
afterRecord.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The actual price rise immediately shifts LRAS right; nominal contracts determine long-run capacity” in this short run aggregate supply task.
afterRecord.feedback: With wages fixed, higher output prices lower real wage cost and encourage output along SRAS. Later higher nominal wages/expected prices change the schedule rather than repeating the same movement.

changes.rationale: Remove an unused worker count; preserve the later checkpoint’s two-horizon task.
changes.economicsRationale: The sticky-wage comparison is unchanged.

beforeRecord.q: Existing tax and benefit rules reduce taxes by $120 and raise benefits in a recession. A separate new purchases bill is passed later. Which classification explains the two stabilization channels?
options: Existing-rule responses are automatic stabilizers; the newly enacted purchases change is discretionary
Both are discretionary because all budget amounts changed
Both are automatic because both affect aggregate demand
Existing-rule responses are monetary policy; only the new bill is fiscal
beforeRecord.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both are discretionary because all budget amounts changed” in this stabilization policy task.
beforeRecord.feedback: Automatic versus discretionary concerns whether new policy action is needed, not whether a budget amount or aggregate demand changes. Existing progressive taxes/benefits respond automatically.

afterRecord.q: An economy has returned to potential output. At the current price level, a delayed purchases program would raise aggregate demand by $60 billion after all multiplier effects. Automatic stabilizers would reduce it by $20 billion, with no other changes. Does their response fully offset the program?
options: AD rises $40 billion; the program is only partly offset.
AD rises $80 billion; both changes add to demand.
AD is unchanged; automatic stabilizers fully offset the program.
AD falls $40 billion; automatic stabilizers more than offset the program.
afterRecord.commonError: Assuming automatic stabilizers fully cancel a delayed discretionary program, or adding effects that have opposite signs.
afterRecord.feedback: The stated total effects give a net AD increase of $60 billion − $20 billion = $40 billion. Automatic stabilizers offset only part of the delayed program, so it can still add demand pressure after output has returned to potential.

changes.rationale: Replace a duplicate classification task with calculation and interpretation of a delayed fiscal expansion partly offset by automatic stabilizers; preserve the policy-mix/overheating repair skill.
changes.economicsRationale: The total demand effects are already multiplied: +60−20=+40. With output initially at potential, automatic stabilizers only partly offset the delayed expansion. No second multiplication applies.

beforeRecord.q: A fixed basket costs $260 in the base year, $312 this year and $343.2 next year. A report treats the increase in CPI index points as the inflation rate. What are next year's CPI and inflation rate?
options: The next CPI is 132; next inflation is 32%
The next CPI is 132; next inflation is 10%
The next CPI is 132; next inflation is 12%
The next CPI is 120; next inflation is 10%
beforeRecord.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The next CPI is 132; next inflation is 32%” in this cpi and inflation measurement task.
beforeRecord.feedback: CPI levels are 120 and 132. Inflation is (132−120)/120×100 = 10%, not the 12-point change or the 32% cumulative rise.

afterRecord.q: The CPI rises from 120 to 132. The statistical agency then makes the first of these years the base year, using the same fixed basket. What are the rebased indexes and the inflation rate, and does rebasing change measured inflation?
options: 100 and 112; inflation rises to 12%.
100 and 110; inflation remains 10%.
100 and 132; inflation rises to 32%.
120 and 132; inflation remains 12%.
afterRecord.commonError: Confusing index-point changes with percentage inflation or treating rebasing as a price change.
afterRecord.feedback: Multiply both indexes by 100/120. They become 100 and 110. Inflation is 132/120 − 1 = 110/100 − 1 = 10%; choosing a new index base does not change the price change.

changes.rationale: Make the later CPI checkpoint test rebasing and interpretation instead of another basket-price substitution.
changes.economicsRationale: 132/120−1=10%; rebasing multiplies both indexes by 100/120, giving 100 and 110 without changing inflation.

beforeRecord.q: A fixed basket includes 260 units of a food whose price rises sharply. Households switch toward a cheaper substitute while maintaining utility. What does the fixed-basket index miss, and how does that affect a payment fully indexed to it?
options: It fully reflects the new choices; the indexed payment must exactly preserve every household's utility
It counts the substitute twice; the index necessarily falls despite the dearer original food
It misses cost-saving substitution; the indexed payment can exceed the increase in minimum cost of maintaining utility
It misses cost-saving substitution; the indexed payment necessarily falls short of that increase
beforeRecord.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It fully reflects the new choices; the indexed payment must exactly preserve every household's utility” in this cpi bias task.
beforeRecord.feedback: Pricing the unchanged basket can overstate the cost increase when consumers substitute to maintain utility. Indexing to that measure can overcompensate relative to the minimum cost-of-living increase.

afterRecord.q: A new product gives households an inexpensive alternative that did not previously exist, but the CPI basket will not include it for several years. Which cost-of-living benefit may the index initially miss?
options: The rise in prices of older products already in the basket.
The change in quantities when the fixed basket is priced again.
The benefit of satisfying wants through an expanded set of choices.
The automatic doubling of purchasing power from any new product.
afterRecord.commonError: Ignoring the cost-of-living benefit of newly available choices.
afterRecord.feedback: A newly available good can let households achieve a given level of satisfaction at lower cost. Delayed inclusion can miss that benefit of expanded choice, a source of new-goods bias.

changes.rationale: Align the new-goods-bias checkpoint and its repair skill, replacing an unrelated substitution-bias duplicate.
changes.economicsRationale: A price index that omits a newly available good may miss the benefit of expanded choice; no claim that every price falls.

beforeRecord.q: A product originally costs $270. Its replacement costs 20% more but provides twice the measured service, with no other relevant quality changes. How should the price change be interpreted after allowing for the improved service?
options: The comparable price rises 20%; improved service should have no role in measuring a like-for-like price.
The price per unit of service falls; counting the entire sticker-price increase as inflation ignores the quality improvement.
The comparable price is unchanged; a new version is always treated as having the old price.
The price per unit of service doubles; the quality gain should be added to rather than allowed for in the comparison.
beforeRecord.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Holding service quality constant; comparable-price measurement should ignore quality” in this cpi bias task.
beforeRecord.feedback: The replacement's price per service unit is 1.20/2 = 0.60 of the old level. A like-for-like comparison must adjust for quality rather than automatically calling the full 20% higher price inflation.

afterRecord.q: A replacement appliance costs 20% more but provides twice the measured service, with no other relevant quality change. How does its price per unit of service compare with the old appliance?
options: It is 20% higher.
It is 40% lower.
It is 60% lower.
It is 80% higher.
afterRecord.commonError: Treating a sticker-price increase as inflation without adjusting for service quality.
afterRecord.feedback: For the same service, the relative price is 1.20/2 = 0.60. Price per unit of service falls 40%, even though the sticker price rises 20%.

changes.rationale: Turn a repeated quality-change interpretation into a short calculation and interpretation.
changes.economicsRationale: Price per service unit changes by 1.20/2=0.60, a 40% decrease.

beforeRecord.q: A discovery increases available mineral resources for 330 workers, but extraction technology and transport remain inadequate. Which policy diagnosis best connects resources to productivity?
options: The resource alone guarantees an immediate proportional increase in output per worker
Transport affects consumption only and cannot limit production from resources
Resource abundance makes worker skills and institutions irrelevant to long-run output
The resource expands potential opportunities, but complementary technology/infrastructure can be the binding constraint
beforeRecord.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The resource alone guarantees an immediate proportional increase in output per worker” in this sources of productivity task.
beforeRecord.feedback: Natural resources can support production, but usable technology, skills and infrastructure determine whether they can be exploited productively. More resources alone need not raise current output.

afterRecord.q: A factory discovers a production method that yields more output with the same workers and equipment. Which source of productivity growth does this illustrate?
options: More physical capital per worker.
An increase in natural resources.
A larger labor force.
Improved technological knowledge.
afterRecord.commonError: Confusing improved production methods with more physical inputs.
afterRecord.feedback: A better method raises output from existing inputs. This is improved technological knowledge rather than an increase in the amount of labor or equipment.

changes.rationale: Use a direct technology task for the first checkpoint and its technological-knowledge repair skill.
changes.economicsRationale: More output from unchanged labor and equipment reflects improved methods, rather than capital deepening.

beforeRecord.q: Of 600 adults, 300 are employed and 30 are unemployed and actively looking for work. A survey also finds 30 people who want work but have stopped searching. A report counts all jobless people as unemployed. How should the unemployment rate and labor-force participation rate be calculated instead?
options: Exclude discouraged workers from unemployment and the labor force; UR is about 9.1% and LFPR is 55%
Include discouraged workers in unemployment; UR is about 16.7% and LFPR is 60%
Include discouraged workers only in the labor force; UR is about 8.3% and LFPR is 60%
Exclude discouraged workers but divide unemployment by adult population; UR is 5% and LFPR is 50%
beforeRecord.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Include discouraged workers in unemployment; UR is about 16.7% and LFPR is 60%” in this unemployment measurement task.
beforeRecord.feedback: The labor force is 300+30 = 330. The discouraged are not active searchers. UR = 0.1/1.1 ≈ 9.1%; LFPR = 1.1/2 = 55%.

afterRecord.q: An economy has 300 employed and 30 unemployed people. Thirty employed people lose their jobs and immediately begin actively seeking work. No one enters or leaves the labor force. What happens to the unemployment rate?
options: It rises from about 9.1% to about 18.2%.
It stays at about 9.1% because the labor force is unchanged.
It rises from 10% to 20% because employment is the denominator.
It falls from about 9.1% to about 8.3% because the labor force grows.
afterRecord.commonError: Using employment as the unemployment-rate denominator or assuming job loss increases the labor force.
afterRecord.feedback: Initially, UR = 30/(300+30) ≈ 9.1%. Job losses move 30 people from employment to unemployment without changing the labor force: UR = 60/330 ≈ 18.2%.

changes.rationale: Test employment-to-unemployment flows at the existing Medium checkpoint instead of duplicating a discouraged-worker classification item.
changes.economicsRationale: Employment falls from 300 to 270 and unemployment rises from 30 to 60; labor force stays 330 and UR=18.18%.
